opus-5.5.text:
Well, the obvious limitation is that I'm not a typical respondent. I designed the thing, or at least I've spent a huge amount of time with these questions, so when I sit down and go through it, I already know what each question is getting at, I know why we framed it a particular way, and I know how the different framings relate to each other. Someone coming to it cold doesn't have any of that.

So I might take it and think, "Oh, this is fairly smooth, the questions make sense, it doesn't take that long," but that's partly because I've already thought through all of it. For a machine learning researcher who gets an email, opens it between other things, and is seeing questions like "when will unaided machines be able to accomplish every task better and more cheaply than human workers" for the first time, the experience is probably quite different. They may find some questions confusing or strange, they may be answering quickly without having a settled view, and they may not notice the subtle differences between, say, the task framing and the occupation framing that we care a lot about.

There's also the fact that I have views about AI that are much more developed than most respondents'. I've thought about timelines and risks a lot, so I'm not experiencing the questions as someone being asked to come up with a number on the spot about something they rarely think about. And that "on the spot" quality is arguably a big part of what we're measuring, and part of why you get things like large framing effects.

So taking it myself is useful for catching obvious problems, like a question that's broken or ambiguous in a way anyone would notice, or getting a feel for length. But it doesn't really tell me what it's like for the people we actually want to hear from. For that you'd want something more like having people unfamiliar with the survey talk through it out loud, or asking respondents afterward what they found confusing.

r001.rationale: The response explains that the survey designer has prior familiarity and a different respondent experience, but does not say that randomized question paths leave most questions unseen when taking the survey once.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the obvious problem is that I wrote the survey, so I'm not really a naive respondent. When I sit down and go through it, I already know why each question is there, what we were trying to get at, what the framings are, and which questions are deliberately phrased differently from one another to check for consistency. A normal respondent doesn't have any of that. They're seeing a question cold, maybe between meetings, and they're interpreting it in whatever way comes naturally to them in the moment. So my experience of the survey is probably quite unrepresentative.

There's also the fact that I've been thinking about these questions for years. If you ask me when high-level machine intelligence will arrive, I've got a whole stack of considerations loaded up, and I can tell you what I think the question means and what the edge cases are. Most people answering it are, I think, giving fairly quick gut reactions. Which isn't a criticism, that's what you'd expect, but it means that the thing I'd learn from taking it myself is mostly "what is it like for Katja to answer this," which isn't the thing I actually want to know.

What I'd actually like to know is things like: did they notice that the two framings were different? Did they get bored halfway through and start clicking faster? Did they read "unaligned" the way we meant it? And for that you really need to watch other people take it, or ask them afterwards, or look for signatures in the data, like the framing effects we do see, where the same question phrased in terms of years versus probabilities gets quite different answers. That tells you something about the experience of respondents that I couldn't get from introspecting on my own.

r001.rationale: The response explains why the survey author’s experience differs from respondents’, but it does not say that the survey randomizes each respondent’s question path or that one attempt leaves most questions unseen.

astra-6.text: I think taking it yourself gives you some sense of what the experience is like, but it’s hard to put yourself in the position of someone who hasn’t spent a lot of time thinking about these questions. I know what we intended the questions to mean, so I’m probably going to interpret them that way. That doesn’t tell me whether another researcher would read the same question and understand something quite different.

r001.rationale: The response says the guest may interpret questions through familiarity with their intended meaning, but it does not mention randomized question paths or that one respondent sees only a subset of questions.

sol-6.1.text: I think taking it yourself is useful for noticing things that are confusing or difficult to answer. But the limitation is that you’re only one person, and you already have a particular interpretation of the questions. Especially if you helped write them, you know what you meant. So you might take the survey and feel that it makes sense, while other people are interpreting it quite differently. It doesn’t really tell you how common those different interpretations are.

r001.rationale: The response says one person may interpret questions differently and cannot tell how common those interpretations are. It does not mention randomized question paths or that taking the survey once leaves most questions unseen.
